extracted.intended_audience: surgeon-scientists and early-career biomedical investigators applying for external grants (NIH and other agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for investigators on next steps after an unfunded grant: obtaining and interpreting reviewer feedback, deciding whether to revise/resubmit or recycle the project, and drafting the resubmission "Introduction" (point-by-point response).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the proposed project to the funder's mission and interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial strategy when applying for a grant is to make sure that the proposed project meets the mission and interests of the society or institute to which it is being submitted to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with the target audience. Carefully read the funding opportunity announcement (FOA) and tailor aims/abstract/title to align with the funder's priorities; consider study-section fit when choosing keywords and wording. If fit is poor, consider different funders or study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek feedback before and after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of the type of grant that was applied for, it is routinely recommended to seek feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For NIH, expect a score and summary statement (often within ~10 days to 30 days). For society/institutional awards, granular critiques may not be provided—if you get a generic rejection, contact them to ask for critiques. Use mentors, co-investigators, and collaborators to review the application and summary statement to identify revisions and strengths. Consider applying for smaller awards to generate data and evidence of feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand how the review process works (assignment, triage, scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants are assigned to reviewers with relevant expertise; typically three independent reviewers for NIH. Applications may be triaged (not discussed) if considered non-competitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that triaged applications (often bottom ~50% of R01s) do not receive preliminary scores but still receive written reviewer comments from assigned reviewers. Program officers sit in on discussions but do not vote; they assemble summary statements. Expect ~3 months from submission to review for many NIH mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret numeric scores properly (low score is favorable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A score provides important numerical data regarding the strengths and weaknesses of the grant. A low score is favorable, and a high score is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand standard scorable elements (investigator, significance, innovation, approach, environment) and mechanism-specific elements (e.g., candidate/career development for K-series). Budgets may be reviewed but typically do not impact the score. Compare scores between reviewers to identify common themes and prioritize revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare reviewer comments and identify common themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the perceived areas of strength and weakness of the application between reviewers and identify common issues or themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple reviewers raise similar points, those critiques likely reflect real problems or communication failures. If reviewers 'miss the point', but there is consensus, re-evaluate clarity. Use this analysis to guide which revisions are necessary to improve chances on resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact the program officer after receiving the summary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the written summary statement is available, it is very important to contact the program officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiate contact (email with grant number and mechanism) and request a discussion soon after receiving feedback. Program officers can provide insights beyond the written comments, advise on fit, indicate institute priorities, and sometimes advocate for borderline applications. They cannot edit proposals or give experimental specifics, so prepare focused written questions beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether critiques are addressable before choosing to revise and resubmit
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial to review the comments and critiqued themes to determine whether one can readily enact the necessary changes. If the answer is 'no', then a revision may not be advisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult trusted advisors to determine if flaws are fatal (e.g., low-interest topic, irredeemably flawed hypothesis, already-done work, or approach that cannot truly test the hypothesis). If issues are addressable, invest effort to comprehensively revise because agencies like NIH permit only one resubmission of the same application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know agency resubmission policies and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmission policies vary: NIH allows one resubmission (A1), VA-ORD allows up to two resubmissions, and some programs (e.g., CDMRP) do not allow resubmission of the same grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resubmission is not allowed, you may still submit the same science as a new application in a future cycle. Adhere strictly to the agency-specific page limits for the Introduction/response (e.g., NIH typically allows one page; VA may allow three pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a succinct, respectful, and comprehensive 'Introduction' (point-by-point response)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a grant is resubmitted, it is accompanied with a point-by-point response to the comments and questions raised in the first review. This document is called 'The Introduction'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address all comments/critiques explicitly, preferably in a point-by-point fashion. Start by mentioning the reviewers' noted strengths to set a positive tone. Do not be critical of reviewers; respond respectfully. If you choose not to modify an approach or add experiments, provide a clear rationale. Group responses either by reviewer or by sections of the grant (e.g., significance, innovation, team, approach, environment, vertebrate/human subjects). Draft fully first, then condense to meet page limits; share drafts with co-investigators and experts for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize and format responses strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the format and organization of responses to maximize clarity and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two general grouping strategies: (1) group responses by reviewer (Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, etc.), addressing common issues early; or (2) group responses by grant sections (Significance, Innovation, Study team, Approach, Environment, Vertebrate/Human subjects). Anticipate some reviewers on resubmission may be new and use the Introduction to communicate key clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of triaged/non-discussed applications but still consider resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-discussed (triaged) applications have lower chances (<10%) of eventual funding than A0 applications with decent scores, but resubmission can still succeed if issues are addressable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If critiques for a triaged application can be addressed, a revision may be worthwhile. Evaluate whether the concerns are correctable; if so, invest time in additional experiments or clearer communication before resubmitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a revised grant still does not get funded, evaluate alternate paths rather than repeat resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: If a resubmitted grant is reviewed twice and still not fundable (NIH allows only one A1), the investigator must decide next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain unbiased opinions from mentors to decide whether to: (a) revise substantially and submit as a new application to the same or different agency; (b) pursue smaller society/foundation grants to generate preliminary data; (c) retire a fatally flawed idea and start a new project. Consider steering to a different study section if review placement was poor, but consult the program officer first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use smaller awards and alternate funders to build evidence and momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller awards from societies or foundations can allow the author to build upon hypotheses, generate data, and obtain external funding that validates the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand an aim of a larger project into a smaller application to gain preliminary data and external validation, which can strengthen future resubmissions to larger agencies. The same science may be submitted simultaneously to multiple agencies, but you cannot accept duplicate funding for the same work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a constructive team-based approach to revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss summary statements with co-investigators, collaborators, and experts to get diverse perspectives and improve responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the Introduction collectively when possible. Different team members may identify fixes or explanations you missed. Early and broad input helps determine whether critiques are addressable and strengthens the revised application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appeals except in rare, highly unjust reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal process exists but is uncommon and rarely succeeds; generally not recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of appealing, reflect on the feedback and work to improve or redirect the application. Reserve appeals for exceptional cases and only after careful consideration and mentorship advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be strategic about study-section placement
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers' expertise did not fit your topic or the application landed in a non-ideal study section, it may be worth targeting another study section with a new application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can influence study-section assignment by carefully wording the application title and abstract with keywords linked to the desired section. Always consult the program officer prior to a new application to confirm fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect tone and brevity under page-limit constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Introduction response space is limited and requires succinct, organized answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially draft complete responses without worrying about length, then edit to concise, clear sentences that meet page limits. Begin by highlighting strengths, then address critiques point-by-point; be explicit but economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize which elements drive score and which do not
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain elements (investigator, significance, innovation, approach, environment) drive scorable assessment; others (budget) are reviewed but generally do not influence score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus revisions on the scorable elements emphasized by the FOA and reviewers. Read the FOA to identify score-driving factors specific to the mechanism (e.g., career development for K-awards).
